radar.title: Sustainable Multi-Zone Greenhouse Fertigation Through Reliability-Aware Sensing, Spatiotemporal Graph Learning, and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
radar.summary: With protected agriculture increasingly developing toward large-scale, multi-zone, and intelligent production, reducing water and fertilizer consumption, drainage losses, and energy waste while maintaining crop yield, product quality, and long-term economic profitability has become an important challenge for sustainable greenhouse production. To address sensor abnormalities, spatial heterogeneity among irrigation zones, competition for shared hydraulic resources, and the limited ability of conventional control strategies to jointly optimize resource efficiency and economic performance, a sensor-driven spatiotemporal graph multi-agent reinforcement learning framework, termed SensorGraph-FertiMARL, is proposed for state sensing, response prediction, and sustainable coordinated fertigation optimization in multi-zone greenhouses. Reliable zone-level states are first obtained through sensor-reliability gating, missing-state reconstruction, and multi-relational graph fusion incorporating spatial, hydraulic, and microclimatic relationships. An action-conditioned fertigation–yield–quality–profit digital twin is then constructed to jointly predict root-zone responses, resource consumption, marketable yield, product quality, and net profit associated with candidate control actions. Finally, graph-based multi-agent proximal policy optimization (Graph-MAPPO) with capacity, safety, and fairness constraints is employed to coordinate fertigation allocation among multiple zones under shared pump, main-pipeline, and nutrient-solution resource constraints. Evaluated through rigorous offline digital-twin simulation and replay testing calibrated against complete multi-stage historical dataset records from an eight-zone commercial greenhouse, experimental results show that the proposed method reduced water and fertilizer use to 75.8% and 78.3% (achieving water and fertilizer saving rates of 24.2% and 21.7%), respectively, relative to the uniform timer-based control baseline, while decreasing the drainage rate to 7.2%. The Grade-A product rate increased to 84.6%, net profit reached 138.9% of the baseline level (a +38.9% net-profit improvement), return on investment (ROI) reached 1.94, and the stress-violation rate was limited to 2.9%. For state sensing and digital-twin prediction, the sensor-state reconstruction mean absolute error (MAE) and coefficient of determination (R2) were 0.036 and 0.918, respectively; the water-content prediction MAE was 0.041, the electrical conductivity (EC) prediction root mean squared error (RMSE) was 0.119, and the drainage prediction mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) was 8.7%. In addition, the R2 for marketable-yield prediction reached 0.912, the macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1) score for quality-grade prediction reached 0.851, the R2 for net-profit prediction reached 0.904, the mean prediction interval width (MPIW) was 0.142, and the prediction interval coverage probability (PICP) reached 0.931. These results demonstrate that SensorGraph-FertiMARL can simultaneously achieve water and fertilizer conservation, drainage reduction, operational-risk control, and economic improvement while maintaining marketable production and quality, thereby providing an effective intelligent optimization approach for resource-efficient, environmentally sustainable, and economically viable greenhouse production.

radar.title: Coverage-Aware Routing with Approximate Equilibrium Guarantees for Location-Diversity Vehicular Crowdsensing
radar.summary: Vehicular crowdsensing uses the sensors of everyday vehicles to monitor cities, but traffic concentrates on few roads, leaving much of the network unsensed. Location-diversity incentives pay vehicles more to travel where few others go, but our earlier mechanism sets how far each vehicle deviates without optimizing collective coverage in route selection. We add this step in two stages. First, a non-cooperative game with diversity-weighted rewards yields each vehicle's equilibrium deviation. Second, the platform recommends to each vehicle a feasible route whose deviation is within a tolerance of this value, chosen to improve coverage. The coverage gain is monotone submodular, so a greedy router with local search attains at least half of the optimal gain over generated candidates. If every active vehicle has a candidate within a tolerance that is small relative to the aggregate deviation, the recommended routes form an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium, with $\varepsilon$ first order in the tolerance, or second order under a stronger condition. On London and Monaco road networks, the router achieves 99.4% and 98.9% of the optimal reduction in the coverage penalty on small instances and exceeds closest-length selection by up to 27.9 points. Under heterogeneous costs, uniform deviation needs compensation averaging 42% of the budget to give every vehicle nonnegative utility; the equilibrium targets need almost none. They also yield more coverage per unit of added travel in most settings and up to 22.6 more points at small budgets, an advantage that depends on placement and reverses at large budgets, where detour limits bind.

radar.title: Beyond Named Mechanisms: Economic Institutions as a Design Space for Artificial Agents
radar.summary: Multiagent research inherited its economic vocabulary of auctions, markets, prices, bargaining, and matching from a single observed case: human societies. Those institutions bundle identity, competence, execution, ownership, commitment, and settlement in ways that suit agents whose minds are private, who learn rather than copy skills, and who each persist as one person. Engineered agents need not share any of these constraints, making the list of familiar institutions look less like the entirety of economic organization and more like a sample from a larger, unmapped space. We sketch one way to make that space concrete: a provisional chart that records each institution, separately from the agents that run it, as a typed structure over positions, rights and duties, allocation, information, time, state, process, value, and external recognition. In this chart, named institutions become overlapping regions rather than fixed points, neighboring families separate along a few coordinates, and the gaps between them become places to search. We show what the shift in perspective buys with a simulation in which one technical act, copying an agent's competence, is institutionalized as a new independent supplier, as licensed capacity that creates no new participant, and as the splitting of one economic position into successors that inherit some obligations and not others. In a paired task, all three produce an identical technical trace despite differing in who exists, who owns the copy, who is obligated, and who gets paid. We close with a research program: building a principled chart of institution space, mapping how its implementable region shifts with agent capacities, and revising the chart wherever engineered agents expose distinctions it cannot express.

radar.title: SELFISH AND COOPERATIVE BEHAVIOUR IN NONATOMIC CONGESTION GAMES
radar.summary: The paper examines the influence of cooperative behavior on the players' population assignment among alternatives in a non-atomic congestion game with affine cost functions. The formulation of the congestion game is proposed in which the player population consists not only of individualists but also of players acting in the interests of a cooperating group. In this formulation, a Nash equilibrium is explicitly obtained, allowing us to analyze the interdependence and interaction of strategies for assigning players among alternatives in a non-atomic congestion game with groups of cooperating players. It is proven that the number of alternatives sought by cooperating players is always no less than the number sought by individualists. Moreover, when groups of cooperating players compete in a congestion game, a larger number of alternatives can only be sought by a larger group. Finally, it is shown that the average payoff of a cooperating player is never greater than the payoff of an individualist.

radar.title: Equilibrium Circulation Model Based on a 24-Division Ring and Core Structure: Mathematics of Exploitation Elimination and Maximum Dispersion/Entropy via the Casino Protocol
radar.venue_raw: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
radar.summary: Abstract This paper proposes a novel systemic and geometric equilibrium model aimed at maximizing the sustainability and energy circulation of an entire system. Expanding upon the concept of the maximum value (represented numerically as "2500") yielded by the product of opposing and complementary elements in a dualism, we apply this principle to a multi-element circulation system. This yields a 25-element structure consisting of a "24-division ring plus a core (origin node)" with a strict equal distribution rule of 4% per element. Furthermore, we mathematically prove that this model achieves the absolute upper limit ("global maximum") of distributive fairness and systemic expansion (dispersion/entropy) from the perspectives of Shannon entropy maximization, geometric mean (product) maximization, and spatial isotropy. Additionally, we discuss the self-healing "Casino Protocol," an automated tuning mechanism designed to prevent structural collapse caused by localized energy biases or exploitative structures exceeding critical thresholds.

radar.title: In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?
radar.summary: When Learning About a Match Stalls the Market In many matching markets, participants must investigate whether a match is feasible. When inspection is costly, participants may delay investigating a potential match until both sides have effectively committed. Such caution can cause each side to wait for others to act, creating an “information deadlock.” In their article, “In Which Matching Markets Do Costly Compatibility Inspections Lead to a Deadlock?” Immorlica, Kanoria, and Lu study this problem in random two-sided markets. They characterize how deadlock depends on the market balance, market connectivity, and the chance that inspections succeed. Using statistical physics tools, their analysis identifies phase transitions between deadlock-free and deadlocked markets. The findings offer design guidance: More choice is not always better; match rates are highest at the deadlock phase boundary; and parallel inspections and clearer participant differentiation can reduce the extent to which waiting chains stall the market.

radar.title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
radar.summary: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficiency. Heterogeneity analysis shows that downsizing is concentrated among highly indebted owner households and businesses with volatile cash flows. For each dollar increase in household spending associated with a child turning 18, business expenses decline by $2.26. These findings are consistent with entrepreneurial parents reallocating capital from business investments toward their children’s human capital, as both compete for the same pool of internal family financial resources. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04789 .

radar.title: Before AI Agents Negotiate for Us: A Competitive Tournament of Rule-Based, Search, Optimization, Learned, and Language-Model Negotiators Under Scarcity
radar.summary: Automated bilateral negotiation underlies two-sided matching markets such as freight brokering, where many shippers and carriers negotiate price before a matching mechanism decides who is paired with whom. Prior strategy comparisons typically use isolated one-on-one duels or a single fixed market, so they cannot show how a strategy behaves against several live rivals under a changing balance of supply and demand. We built nine negotiation architectures spanning rule-based, search-based, optimization-based, imitation-learning, and reinforcement-learning families, and ran all nine simultaneously on both sides of a Gale-Shapley matching market under a balanced condition and two scarcity conditions rotated across all 36 exclusion pairs. In the balanced carrier market, an imitation-learned engine (ML2), a reinforcement-learning policy trained only on isolated negotiations (RL), and an expected-utility optimization engine (OPT) formed a statistically tied top group, and no architecture led in every condition and role. RL beat all eight carrier rivals when carriers were scarce, but its match rate collapsed from 62% to 16% when shippers were scarce and it had to compete with the other carrier agents for demand. A second reinforcement-learning policy trained against rival agents (RL2) kept its match rate above 91% in every condition, yet lost on realized payoff to all eight shipper-side rivals in two of the three conditions, traced to a confirmed train/deployment feature mismatch. We also tested nine large language models (LLMs), from 1 to 72 billion parameters, under the same protocol: they lost significantly to the two strongest engines (OPT2 and ML2) in 32 of 36 comparisons and won none. These results show that isolated or single-condition evaluation can hide failure modes that a many-sided, scarcity-varying, statistically corrected tournament exposes directly.

radar.title: Random feature policy iteration for inverse mean field games with complex geometry and high dimensions
radar.summary: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems. The method builds on a policy iteration framework for inverse MFGs, which decouples the coupled nonlinear forward-backward PDE system into a sequence of linear PDE and inverse problem solves. The fixed random feature representations preserve this linear structure, allowing the resulting subproblems to be solved by minimizing residuals at sampled collocation points through linear least-squares problems. The mesh-free nature of the method further extends the applicability of the policy iteration framework to inverse MFGs with complex geometry and in high dimensions. Another key advantage is its flexibility in using different spatial approximations for different variables: the obstacle function, value function, and population density can be represented in separate feature spaces, accommodating obstacles that are substantially less regular than the corresponding PDE solutions. Moreover, boundary conditions can be enforced through collocation on irregular domains without constructing boundary-fitted meshes. Numerical experiments involving smooth and discontinuous obstacles, a domain with holes, and higher-dimensional problems demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of the proposed method.
radar.summary_short: We propose a random feature policy iteration method for reconstructing the obstacle function in a mean-field game (MFG) from observations of its value function, leveraging the method's mesh-free nature and flexibility to handle complex geometries and high-dimensional problems.

radar.title: Turning Multi-Agent Communication into Token-Level Credit with On Policy Self Distillation
radar.summary: Reinforcement learning improves problem solving in large language model multi-agent systems. Existing approaches overlook communication knowledge or compress it into scalar rewards, leaving coarse credit with little guidance on which decisions each agent should reinforce or revise. OPSD4MAS converts future communication into fine-grained token-level credit through On Policy Self Distillation (OPSD). An external model extracts facts and assesses their trajectory relations for coarse-grained filtering, followed by fine-grained leave-one-out filtering of target-token influence against agent-wise outcome advantages. The fact-conditioned policy supplies token-level credit, combined with GRPO through a linearly annealed joint objective. Our method improves mathematical pass@4 over GRPO by up to 20.00 percentage points. Ablations support complete filtering, while frozen-history injection diagnostics support fact utility. Together, these results support combining agent-level outcome guidance with communication-derived token-level credit. Code is available at https://github.com/Camel-Prince/OPSD4MAS.
